newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan court clears reporters in libel suit.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan court clears reporters in libel suit.

text.p: A Taiwan district court on Tuesday acquitted two reporters and two editorial staffers of a Hong Kong-based magazine in a libel suit seen as a test for free speech in Taiwan.
"After close examination and hearings of the case, we did not think the four were guilty of libel against Liu Tai-ying," judge Lee Wei-hsin told Reuters by telephone.

"Even if it was found later their report was different from the fact, we still ruled that the libel case could not be substantiated as long as the defendants had made reasonable checks of their story," the judge said.

Liu, head of the ruling Nationalist Party's Business Management Committee, filed a libel suit on November 6, 1996 against Chinese-American writer Ying Chan and Taiwan reporter Hsieh Chung-liang of the monthly magazine Yazhou Zhoukan.

Liu also sued the director of the magazine's Taiwan office Wang Shu-yun and its Hong Kong's chief editor Yau Pun-lap over their report that he had offered a former U.S. White House aide, Mark Middleton, a US$15 million-donation to President Bill Clinton's re-election campaign.
The judge said Liu had 10 days to appeal the district court decision. It was not immediately known whether Liu would appeal.
Liu denied that he had ever made the offer. The magazine article touched off a series of cross-examinations of the source of Clinton's campaign funds.
Under the U.S. law, a presidential candidate cannot accept contributions by foreign governments or political organisations.
Taipei district judges said the suit was basically a case of press freedom versus libel law.

"Unlike the old days before martial law was lifted in 1987, press freedom or free speech are respected nowaday. You can criticised anything you like, and rarely your criticism would earn for you a jail term," a court official told Reuters.
Ying Chan, who attended a court hearing last week, said it would discredit Taiwan's system if the judgement went against them.
